question:
You need to train a natural language model to perform text classification on product descriptions that contain millions of examples and 100,000
 unique words. You want to preprocess the words individually so that they can be fed into a recurrent neural network. What should you do?
option_a: Create a hot-encoding of words, and feed the encodings into your model.
option_b: Identify word embeddings from a pre-trained model, and use the embeddings in your model.
option_c: Sort the words by frequency of occurrence, and use the frequencies as the encodings in your model.
option_d: Assign a numerical value to each word from 1 to 100,000 and feed the values as inputs in your model.
explanation: Pretrained word embeddings map words into dense vectors that capture semantic relationships and are far more practical for a 100,000-word vocabulary than one-hot vectors. The embeddings can be used as inputs to the recurrent model and optionally fine-tuned.
exam_section: Collaborating within and across teams to manage data and models
exam_objectives: Exploring and preprocessing data for ML
topics: Embeddings; NLP; Vector Search; Feature Engineering

question:
You work for an online travel agency that also sells advertising placements on its website to other companies. You have been asked to predict the
 most relevant web banner that a user should see next. Security is important to your company. The model latency requirements are 300ms@p99,
 the inventory is thousands of web banners, and your exploratory analysis has shown that navigation context is a good predictor. You want to
 Implement the simplest solution. How should you configure the prediction pipeline?
option_a: Embed the client on the website, and then deploy the model on AI Platform Prediction.
option_b:
Embed the client on the website, deploy the gateway on App Engine, deploy the database on Firestore for writing and for reading the user’s
 navigation context, and then deploy the model on AI Platform Prediction.
option_c:
Embed the client on the website, deploy the gateway on App Engine, deploy the database on Cloud Bigtable for writing and for reading the
 user’s navigation context, and then deploy the model on AI Platform Prediction.
option_d:
Embed the client on the website, deploy the gateway on App Engine, deploy the database on Memorystore for writing and for reading the
 user’s navigation context, and then deploy the model on Google Kubernetes Engine.
explanation: A server-side gateway keeps credentials and model calls off the browser, while Firestore provides a simple managed store for per-user navigation context with low operational overhead. For thousands of banners and a 300 ms p99 target, Firestore is simpler than Bigtable or a self-managed GKE serving stack. This appears to be a newer variant of PMLE-0049 and the correct answer differs because Firestore is explicitly offered.

question:

 autoscaling and monitoring for online prediction requests. Which platform components should you choose for this system?
option_a: Agent Platform Pipelines and App Engine
option_b: Agent Platform Pipelines, Vertex AI Prediction, and Agent Platform Model Monitoring
option_c: Cloud Composer, BigQuery ML, and Vertex AI Prediction
option_d: Cloud Composer, Agent Platform Managed Training with custom containers, and App Engine
explanation: Agent Platform Pipelines can schedule and orchestrate containerized retraining workflows. Vertex AI online prediction provides managed autoscaling, and Agent Platform Model Monitoring detects skew and drift for deployed models. question:
You are profiling the performance of your TensorFlow model training time and notice a performance issue caused by inefficiencies in the input
 data pipeline for a single 5 terabyte CSV file dataset on Cloud Storage. You need to optimize the input pipeline performance. Which action should
 you try first to increase the efficiency of your pipeline?
option_a: Preprocess the input CSV file into a TFRecord file.
option_b: Randomly select a 10 gigabyte subset of the data to train your model.
option_c: Split into multiple CSV files and use a parallel interleave transformation.
option_d: Set the reshuffle_each_iteration parameter to true in the tf.data.Dataset.shuffle method.
explanation: A single 5 TB file prevents the input pipeline from reading multiple files concurrently. Sharding the CSV and using parallel interleave is the first change that enables parallel I/O. Converting to TFRecord may help later, but a single unsharded file would still limit parallelism.

question:
You need to design an architecture that serves asynchronous predictions to determine whether a particular mission-critical machine part will fail.
 Your system collects data from multiple sensors from the machine. You want to build a model that will predict a failure in the next N minutes,
 given the average of each sensor’s data from the past 12 hours. How should you design the architecture?
option_a:
1. HTTP requests are sent by the sensors to your ML model, which is deployed as a microservice and exposes a REST API for prediction
 2. Your application queries a Agent Platform endpoint where you deployed your model.
 3. Responses are received by the caller application as soon as the model produces the prediction.
option_b:
1. Events are sent by the sensors to Pub/Sub, consumed in real time, and processed by a Dataflow stream processing pipeline.
 2. The pipeline invokes the model for prediction and sends the predictions to another Pub/Sub topic.
 3. Pub/Sub messages containing predictions are then consumed by a downstream system for monitoring.
option_c:
1. Export your data to Cloud Storage using Dataflow.
 2. Submit a Agent Platform batch prediction job that uses your trained model in Cloud Storage to perform scoring on the preprocessed data.
 3. Export the batch prediction job outputs from Cloud Storage and import them into Cloud SQL.
option_d:
1. Export the data to Cloud Storage using the BigQuery command-line tool
 2. Submit a Agent Platform batch prediction job that uses your trained model in Cloud Storage to perform scoring on the preprocessed data.
 3. Export the batch prediction job outputs from Cloud Storage and import them into BigQuery.
explanation: The requirement is asynchronous, near-real-time prediction over continuously arriving sensor events. Pub/Sub decouples producers and consumers, while a streaming Dataflow pipeline can maintain the 12-hour aggregates, invoke inference, and publish results to another topic.

question:
Your company manages an application that aggregates news articles from many different online sources and sends them to users. You need to
 build a recommendation model that will suggest articles to readers that are similar to the articles they are currently reading. Which approach
 should you use?
option_a: Create a collaborative filtering system that recommends articles to a user based on the user’s past behavior.
option_b: Encode all articles into vectors using word2vec, and build a model that returns articles based on vector similarity.
option_c: Build a logistic regression model for each user that predicts whether an article should be recommended to a user.
option_d:
Manually label a few hundred articles, and then train an SVM classifier based on the manually classified articles that categorizes additional
 articles into their respective categories.
explanation: This is a content-similarity recommendation problem. Encoding article text into vectors and retrieving nearby vectors recommends articles similar to the one being read, even without relying on each user's history.

topics: Recommendation Systems; Embeddings; Vector Search; Classification

question:
You work for a large social network service provider whose users post articles and discuss news. Millions of comments are posted online each
 day, and more than 200 human moderators constantly review comments and flag those that are inappropriate. Your team is building an ML model
 to help human moderators check content on the platform. The model scores each comment and flags suspicious comments to be reviewed by a
 human. Which metric(s) should you use to monitor the model’s performance?
option_a: Number of messages flagged by the model per minute
option_b: Number of messages flagged by the model per minute confirmed as being inappropriate by humans.
option_c: Precision and recall estimates based on a random sample of 0.1% of raw messages each minute sent to a human for review
option_d: Precision and recall estimates based on a sample of messages flagged by the model as potentially inappropriate each minute
explanation: To estimate both precision and recall, humans must review a representative sample of all messages, including messages the model did not flag. Reviewing only flagged messages can estimate precision but cannot measure false negatives and therefore cannot estimate recall.
exam_objectives: Monitoring, testing, and troubleshooting AI solutions

question:
You are an ML engineer at a bank. You have developed a binary classification model using AutoML Tables to predict whether a customer will make
 loan payments on time. The output is used to approve or reject loan requests. One customer’s loan request has been rejected by your model, and
 the bank’s risks department is asking you to provide the reasons that contributed to the model’s decision. What should you do?
option_a: Use local feature importance from the predictions.
option_b: Use the correlation with target values in the data summary page.
option_c: Use the feature importance percentages in the model evaluation page.
option_d: Vary features independently to identify the threshold per feature that changes the classification.
explanation: The bank needs an explanation for one specific rejected application. Local feature importance, or local feature attribution, explains how each feature contributed to that individual prediction. Global feature importance does not explain a single decision.

question:
You work for a magazine distributor and need to build a model that predicts which customers will renew their subscriptions for the upcoming year.
 Using your company’s historical data as your training set, you created a TensorFlow model and deployed it to AI Platform. You need to determine
 which customer attribute has the most predictive power for each prediction served by the model. What should you do?
option_a:
Use AI Platform notebooks to perform a Lasso regression analysis on your model, which will eliminate features that do not provide a strong
 signal.
option_b:
Stream prediction results to BigQuery. Use BigQuery’s CORR(X1, X2) function to calculate the Pearson correlation coefficient between each
 feature and the target variable.
option_c:
Use the AI Explanations feature on AI Platform. Submit each prediction request with the ‘explain’ keyword to retrieve feature attributions
 using the sampled Shapley method.
option_d:
Use the What-If tool in Google Cloud to determine how your model will perform when individual features are excluded. Rank the feature
 importance in order of those that caused the most significant performance drop when removed from the model.
explanation: Feature attributions from Explainable AI identify the contribution of each input feature to an individual served prediction. Sampled Shapley is suitable for tabular models. Correlation and global feature-removal tests do not provide per-prediction explanations.

topics: Explainability; Online Inference; BigQuery; Workbench

question:
You are working on a binary classification ML algorithm that detects whether an image of a classified scanned document contains a company’s
 logo. In the dataset, 96% of examples don’t have the logo, so the dataset is very skewed. Which metrics would give you the most confidence in
 your model?
option_a: F-score where recall is weighed more than precision
option_b: RMSE
option_c: F-score where precision is weighed more than recall
option_d: F1 score
explanation: For a strongly imbalanced binary classifier, F1 combines precision and recall and is more informative than accuracy or RMSE. The question does not state that false negatives are more costly than false positives, so there is not enough justification to weight recall more heavily. If missing a logo is explicitly more costly, an F-beta score with beta greater than 1 would be appropriate.

question:
You work on the data science team for a multinational beverage company. You need to develop an ML model to predict the company’s profitability
 for a new line of naturally flavored bottled waters in different locations. You are provided with historical data that includes product types, product
 sales volumes, expenses, and profits for all regions. What should you use as the input and output for your model?
option_a: Use latitude, longitude, and product type as features. Use profit as model output.
option_b: Use latitude, longitude, and product type as features. Use revenue and expenses as model outputs.
option_c: Use product type and the feature cross of latitude with longitude, followed by binning, as features. Use profit as model output.
option_d:
Use product type and the feature cross of latitude with longitude, followed by binning, as features. Use revenue and expenses as model
 outputs.
explanation: Profit is the required prediction target. Geographic effects are usually more useful when latitude and longitude are bucketized and crossed, allowing the model to learn local interactions instead of treating raw coordinates as independent linear quantities.

question:
You work on an operations team at an international company that manages a large fleet of on-premises servers located in few data centers
 around the world. Your team collects monitoring data from the servers, including CPU/memory consumption. When an incident occurs on a server,
 your team is responsible for fixing it. Incident data has not been properly labeled yet. Your management team wants you to build a predictive
 maintenance solution that uses monitoring data from the VMs to detect potential failures and then alerts the service desk team. What should you
 do first?
option_a:
Train a time-series model to predict the machines’ performance values. Configure an alert if a machine’s actual performance values
 significantly differ from the predicted performance values.
option_b:
Implement a simple heuristic (e.g., based on z-score) to label the machines’ historical performance data. Train a model to predict
 anomalies based on this labeled dataset.
option_c:
Develop a simple heuristic (e.g., based on z-score) to label the machines’ historical performance data. Test this heuristic in a production
 environment.
option_d:
Hire a team of qualified analysts to review and label the machines’ historical performance data. Train a model based on this manually
 labeled dataset.
explanation: Because reliable labels do not yet exist, begin with a simple anomaly heuristic and validate it in production. This establishes whether the signal is useful and creates evidence for later labeling and model development before investing in an expensive supervised solution.

question:
You are training an object detection machine learning model on a dataset that consists of three million X-ray images, each roughly 2 GB in size.
 You are using Agent Platform Managed Training to run a custom training application on a Compute Engine instance with 32-cores, 128 GB of RAM, and 1 NVIDIA
 P100 GPU. You notice that model training is taking a very long time. You want to decrease training time without sacrificing model performance.
 What should you do?
option_a: Increase the instance memory to 512 GB and increase the batch size.
option_b: Replace the NVIDIA P100 GPU with a v3-32 TPU in the training job.
option_c: Enable early stopping in your Agent Platform Managed Training job.
option_d: Use the tf.distribute.Strategy API and run a distributed training job.
explanation: The workload is extremely large, so the first scalable approach is distributed training with tf.distribute.Strategy across multiple workers and accelerators. Merely adding host memory or enabling early stopping does not improve full-training throughput, and replacing the GPU with a TPU without profiling or adapting the input pipeline is not guaranteed to help.

You are developing an ML model intended to classify whether X-ray images indicate bone fracture risk. You have trained a ResNet architecture on
 Vertex AI using a TPU as an accelerator, however you are unsatisfied with the training time and memory usage. You want to quickly iterate your
 training code but make minimal changes to the code. You also want to minimize impact on the model’s accuracy. What should you do?
option_a: Reduce the number of layers in the model architecture.
option_b: Reduce the global batch size from 1024 to 256.
option_c: Reduce the dimensions of the images used in the model.
option_d: Configure your model to use bfloat16 instead of float32.

You have successfully deployed to production a large and complex TensorFlow model trained on tabular data. You want to predict the lifetime
 value (LTV) field for each subscription stored in the BigQuery table named subscription. subscriptionPurchase in the project named my-
 fortune500-company-project.
 You have organized all your training code, from preprocessing data from the BigQuery table up to deploying the validated model to the Vertex AI
 endpoint, into a TensorFlow Extended (TFX) pipeline. You want to prevent prediction drift, i.e., a situation when a feature data distribution in
 production changes significantly over time. What should you do?
option_a: Implement continuous retraining of the model daily using Agent Platform Pipelines.
option_b: Add a model monitoring job where 10% of incoming predictions are sampled 24 hours.
option_c: Add a model monitoring job where 90% of incoming predictions are sampled 24 hours.
option_d: Add a model monitoring job where 10% of incoming predictions are sampled every hour.
explanation: Model monitoring detects drift; it does not literally prevent it. Of the listed configurations, sampling 10% every hour provides the most timely drift signal while controlling monitoring cost. A 24-hour interval delays detection, and sampling 90% is usually unnecessarily expensive.

question:
You recently developed a deep learning model using Keras, and now you are experimenting with different training strategies. First, you trained the
 model using a single GPU, but the training process was too slow. Next, you distributed the training across 4 GPUs using
 tf.distribute.MirroredStrategy (with no other changes), but you did not observe a decrease in training time. What should you do?
option_a: Distribute the dataset with tf.distribute.Strategy.experimental_distribute_dataset
option_b: Create a custom training loop.
option_c: Use a TPU with tf.distribute.TPUStrategy.
option_d: Increase the batch size.
explanation: MirroredStrategy splits each global batch across replicas. With the original batch size, each GPU may receive too little work for the synchronization overhead to be worthwhile. Increasing the global batch size improves accelerator utilization and can deliver scaling, with learning-rate tuning as needed.

question:
You work for a gaming company that has millions of customers around the world. All games offer a chat feature that allows players to
 communicate with each other in real time. Messages can be typed in more than 20 languages and are translated in real time using the Cloud
 Translation API. You have been asked to build an ML system to moderate the chat in real time while assuring that the performance is uniform
 across the various languages and without changing the serving infrastructure.
 You trained your first model using an in-house word2vec model for embedding the chat messages translated by the Cloud Translation API.
 However, the model has significant differences in performance across the different languages. How should you improve it?
option_a: Add a regularization term such as the Min-Diff algorithm to the loss function.
option_b: Train a classifier using the chat messages in their original language.
option_c: Replace the in-house word2vec with GPT-3 or T5.
option_d: Remove moderation for languages for which the false positive rate is too high.
explanation: MinDiff regularization is designed to reduce performance disparities between defined data slices while retaining the same model-serving architecture. Training independent handling for original-language messages would require a multilingual input and embedding path and could change the serving flow. The language groups and fairness metric still need careful definition.

question:
You are experimenting with a built-in distributed XGBoost model in Agent Platform Workbench user-managed notebooks. You use BigQuery to split your
 data into training and validation sets using the following queries:
 CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE ‘myproject.mydataset.training‘ AS
 (SELECT * FROM ‘myproject.mydataset.mytable‘ WHERE RAND() <= 0.8);
 CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE ‘myproject.mydataset.validation‘ AS
 (SELECT * FROM ‘myproject.mydataset.mytable‘ WHERE RAND() <= 0.2);
 After training the model, you achieve an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC ROC) value of 0.8, but after deploying the
 model to production, you notice that your model performance has dropped to an AUC ROC value of 0.65. What problem is most likely occurring?
option_a: There is training-serving skew in your production environment.
option_b: There is not a sufficient amount of training data.
option_c:
The tables that you created to hold your training and validation records share some records, and you may not be using all the data in your
 initial table.
option_d:
The RAND() function generated a number that is less than 0.2 in both instances, so every record in the validation table will also be in the
 training table.
explanation: The two RAND() filters are evaluated independently. Some records can appear in both tables, while others can appear in neither, contaminating validation and failing to use the full source table. Generate one stable split key or random value and derive mutually exclusive partitions from it.

question:
During batch training of a neural network, you notice that there is an oscillation in the loss. How should you adjust your model to ensure that it
 converges?
option_a: Decrease the learning rate hyperparameter.
option_b: Decrease the size of the training batch.
option_c: Increase the learning rate hyperparameter.
option_d: Increase the size of the training batch.
explanation: Oscillating loss commonly indicates that optimization steps are overshooting minima. Lowering the learning rate reduces step size and usually stabilizes convergence.
exam_objectives: Training models
topics: Model Optimization; Hyperparameter Tuning; Custom Training

question:
You work for a toy manufacturer that has been experiencing a large increase in demand. You need to build an ML model to reduce the amount of
 time spent by quality control inspectors checking for product defects. Faster defect detection is a priority. The factory does not have reliable Wi-
 Fi. Your company wants to implement the new ML model as soon as possible. Which model should you use?
option_a: AutoML Vision Edge mobile-high-accuracy-1 model
option_b: AutoML Vision Edge mobile-low-latency-1 model
option_c: AutoML Vision model
option_d: AutoML Vision Edge mobile-versatile-1 model
explanation: The factory lacks reliable connectivity, so inference should run on the edge. Because rapid defect detection is the priority, the mobile-low-latency model is the best listed tradeoff. This is a legacy AutoML Vision Edge model name.
exam_objectives: Serving models
topics: Computer Vision; Troubleshooting; AutoML; Evaluation Metrics

question:
You need to build classification workflows over several structured datasets currently stored in BigQuery. Because you will be performing the
 classification several times, you want to complete the following steps without writing code: exploratory data analysis, feature selection, model
 building, training, and hyperparameter tuning and serving. What should you do?
option_a: Train a TensorFlow model on Vertex AI.
option_b: Train a classification Vertex AutoML model.
option_c: Run a logistic regression job on BigQuery ML.
option_d: Use scikit-learn in Notebooks with pandas library.
explanation: Agent Platform AutoML classification provides a managed, largely no-code workflow for data exploration, feature processing, model training, tuning, evaluation, deployment, and serving. BigQuery ML requires SQL and does not provide the same complete no-code workflow.
terminology_notes: Generic or unrecognized Vertex AI reference requires contextual review.
exam_objectives: Developing ML models using BigQuery ML or AutoML on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform

question:
You are an ML engineer in the contact center of a large enterprise. You need to build a sentiment analysis tool that predicts customer sentiment
 from recorded phone conversations. You need to identify the best approach to building a model while ensuring that the gender, age, and cultural
 differences of the customers who called the contact center do not impact any stage of the model development pipeline and results. What should
 you do?
option_a: Convert the speech to text and extract sentiments based on the sentences.
option_b: Convert the speech to text and build a model based on the words.
option_c: Extract sentiment directly from the voice recordings.
option_d: Convert the speech to text and extract sentiment using syntactical analysis.
explanation: Transcribing speech and analyzing sentence-level text removes direct acoustic signals such as voice pitch that can correlate with age or gender and preserves context better than isolated word analysis. This does not by itself guarantee fairness; performance must still be evaluated across demographic and cultural slices.
exam_objectives: Identifying risks to AI solutions; Building AI solutions using Google Cloud AI APIs or foundational models
topics: Responsible AI; Speech-to-Text; Pipelines; NLP

question:
You need to analyze user activity data from your company’s mobile applications. Your team will use BigQuery for data analysis, transformation,
 and experimentation with ML algorithms. You need to ensure real-time ingestion of the user activity data into BigQuery. What should you do?
option_a: Configure Pub/Sub to stream the data into BigQuery.
option_b: Run an Apache Spark streaming job on Dataproc to ingest the data into BigQuery.
option_c: Run a Dataflow streaming job to ingest the data into BigQuery.
option_d: Configure Pub/Sub and a Dataflow streaming job to ingest the data into BigQuery,
explanation: Pub/Sub BigQuery subscriptions can write messages directly into an existing BigQuery table, providing real-time ingestion without a separate Dataflow pipeline when no custom transformation is required. Older versions of this question may have expected Pub/Sub plus Dataflow before BigQuery subscriptions existed.
exam_section: Collaborating within and across teams to manage data and models
exam_objectives: Exploring and preprocessing data for ML

question:
You work for a gaming company that manages a popular online multiplayer game where teams with 6 players play against each other in 5-minute
 battles. There are many new players every day. You need to build a model that automatically assigns available players to teams in real time. User
 research indicates that the game is more enjoyable when battles have players with similar skill levels. Which business metrics should you track to
 measure your model’s performance?
option_a: Average time players wait before being assigned to a team
option_b: Precision and recall of assigning players to teams based on their predicted versus actual ability
option_c: User engagement as measured by the number of battles played daily per user
option_d: Rate of return as measured by additional revenue generated minus the cost of developing a new model
explanation: The goal is to make battles more enjoyable. Daily battles per user is a direct behavioral business outcome that can reveal whether users engage more after improved matchmaking. Wait time is an operational guardrail, while precision and recall require a questionable ground-truth skill label.
exam_objectives: Monitoring, testing, and troubleshooting AI solutions
topics: Evaluation Metrics; Model Monitoring

question:
You are building an ML model to predict trends in the stock market based on a wide range of factors. While exploring the data, you notice that
 some features have a large range. You want to ensure that the features with the largest magnitude don’t overfit the model. What should you do?
option_a: Standardize the data by transforming it with a logarithmic function.
option_b: Apply a principal component analysis (PCA) to minimize the effect of any particular feature.
option_c: Use a binning strategy to replace the magnitude of each feature with the appropriate bin number.
option_d: Normalize the data by scaling it to have values between 0 and 1.
explanation: Min-max normalization places features on a common scale so large numeric magnitudes do not dominate gradient-based training. PCA changes the representation, binning discards detail, and a logarithm is not a general standardization method.
exam_section: Collaborating within and across teams to manage data and models
exam_objectives: Exploring and preprocessing data for ML
topics: Feature Engineering; Regression; Data Preparation

question:
You work for a biotech startup that is experimenting with deep learning ML models based on properties of biological organisms. Your team
 frequently works on early-stage experiments with new architectures of ML models, and writes custom TensorFlow ops in C++. You train your
 models on large datasets and large batch sizes. Your typical batch size has 1024 examples, and each example is about 1 MB in size. The average
 size of a network with all weights and embeddings is 20 GB. What hardware should you choose for your models?
option_a:
A cluster with 2 n1-highcpu-64 machines, each with 8 NVIDIA Tesla V100 GPUs (128 GB GPU memory in total), and a n1-highcpu-64
 machine with 64 vCPUs and 58 GB RAM
option_b:
A cluster with 2 a2-megagpu-16g machines, each with 16 NVIDIA Tesla A100 GPUs (640 GB GPU memory in total), 96 vCPUs, and 1.4 TB
 RAM
option_c: A cluster with an n1-highcpu-64 machine with a v2-8 TPU and 64 GB RAM
option_d: A cluster with 4 n1-highcpu-96 machines, each with 96 vCPUs and 86 GB RAM
explanation: The model is about 20 GB and a 1,024-example batch represents roughly 1 TB of raw input before intermediate activations. The A100 configuration provides by far the largest accelerator and host memory and supports custom TensorFlow workloads. TPUs are not suitable for arbitrary custom C++ TensorFlow operations, while the CPU-only option would be much slower. Exact memory needs still require profiling.
exam_objectives: Choosing appropriate hardware for training
topics: Training Hardware; Embeddings; Experiments; Custom Training

question:
You are an ML engineer at an ecommerce company and have been tasked with building a model that predicts how much inventory the logistics
 team should order each month. Which approach should you take?
option_a:
Use a clustering algorithm to group popular items together. Give the list to the logistics team so they can increase inventory of the popular
 items.
option_b:
Use a regression model to predict how much additional inventory should be purchased each month. Give the results to the logistics team at
 the beginning of the month so they can increase inventory by the amount predicted by the model.
option_c:
Use a time series forecasting model to predict each item's monthly sales. Give the results to the logistics team so they can base inventory
 on the amount predicted by the model.
option_d:
Use a classification model to classify inventory levels as UNDER_STOCKED, OVER_STOCKED, and CORRECTLY_STOCKEGive the report to the
 logistics team each month so they can fine-tune inventory levels.
explanation: Inventory ordering is driven by future demand over time. Forecasting monthly sales per item directly estimates the quantity the logistics team needs, while clustering and classification do not predict a numeric demand trajectory.
exam_objectives: Building models given the task considering cost, complexity, latency, and scalability
topics: Forecasting; Time Series; Classification; Regression

question:
You are building a TensorFlow model for a financial institution that predicts the impact of consumer spending on inflation globally. Due to the size
 and nature of the data, your model is long-running across all types of hardware, and you have built frequent checkpointing into the training
 process. Your organization has asked you to minimize cost. What hardware should you choose?
option_a: A Agent Platform Workbench user-managed notebooks instance running on an n1-standard-16 with 4 NVIDIA P100 GPUs
option_b: A Agent Platform Workbench user-managed notebooks instance running on an n1-standard-16 with an NVIDIA P100 GPU
option_c: A Agent Platform Workbench user-managed notebooks instance running on an n1-standard-16 with a non-preemptible v3-8 TPU
option_d: A Agent Platform Workbench user-managed notebooks instance running on an n1-standard-16 with a preemptible v3-8 TPU
explanation: The job is long-running but already checkpoints frequently, making it tolerant of interruption. Preemptible TPU capacity offers the lowest listed accelerator cost, and checkpoints allow training to resume after reclamation. Modern Google Cloud terminology uses Spot VMs and queued TPU resources rather than this older configuration.
terminology_notes: Applied official direct product-name mappings only.
exam_objectives: Choosing appropriate hardware for training
topics: Training Hardware; Agents; Workbench; Custom Training

question:
You work for a company that provides an anti-spam service that flags and hides spam posts on social media platforms. Your company currently
 uses a list of 200,000 keywords to identify suspected spam posts. If a post contains more than a few of these keywords, the post is identified as
 spam. You want to start using machine learning to flag spam posts for human review. What is the main advantage of implementing machine
 learning for this business case?
option_a: Posts can be compared to the keyword list much more quickly.
option_b: New problematic phrases can be identified in spam posts.
option_c: A much longer keyword list can be used to flag spam posts.
option_d: Spam posts can be flagged using far fewer keywords.
explanation: A learned text model can generalize beyond a fixed keyword list and recognize new phrases and combinations associated with spam. It can therefore surface evolving patterns that were never explicitly added to the rules.
exam_objectives: Building models given the task considering cost, complexity, latency, and scalability
topics: Classification; NLP; Responsible AI

question:
One of your models is trained using data provided by a third-party data broker. The data broker does not reliably notify you of formatting changes
 in the data. You want to make your model training pipeline more robust to issues like this. What should you do?
option_a: Use TensorFlow Data Validation to detect and flag schema anomalies.
option_b:
Use TensorFlow Transform to create a preprocessing component that will normalize data to the expected distribution, and replace values
 that don’t match the schema with 0.
option_c: Use tf.math to analyze the data, compute summary statistics, and flag statistical anomalies.
option_d: Use custom TensorFlow functions at the start of your model training to detect and flag known formatting errors.
explanation: TensorFlow Data Validation infers and validates schemas and flags anomalies such as unexpected types, missing fields, and changed formats before training. Silently replacing malformed values with zero could hide upstream data defects.
exam_objectives: Developing end-to-end ML pipelines; Exploring and preprocessing data for ML
topics: Custom Training; Data Preparation; Pipelines

question:
You work for a company that is developing a new video streaming platform. You have been asked to create a recommendation system that will
 suggest the next video for a user to watch. After a review by an AI Ethics team, you are approved to start development. Each video asset in your
 company’s catalog has useful metadata (e.g., content type, release date, country), but you do not have any historical user event data. How should
 you build the recommendation system for the first version of the product?
option_a:
Launch the product without machine learning. Present videos to users alphabetically, and start collecting user event data so you can
 develop a recommender model in the future.
option_b:
Launch the product without machine learning. Use simple heuristics based on content metadata to recommend similar videos to users, and
 start collecting user event data so you can develop a recommender model in the future.
option_c:
Launch the product with machine learning. Use a publicly available dataset such as MovieLens to train a model using the
 Recommendations AI, and then apply this trained model to your data.
option_d:
Launch the product with machine learning. Generate embeddings for each video by training an autoencoder on the content metadata using
 TensorFlow. Cluster content based on the similarity of these embeddings, and then recommend videos from the same cluster.
explanation: Without user-event history, collaborative recommendation models cannot learn preferences. Content metadata supports a sensible heuristic cold-start experience, while collecting impressions, clicks, and watch events creates the data needed for a later personalized recommender.
exam_objectives: Building models given the task considering cost, complexity, latency, and scalability
topics: Recommendation Systems; Autoscaling; Embeddings; Vector Search

question:
You recently built the first version of an image segmentation model for a self-driving car. After deploying the model, you observe a decrease in the
 area under the curve (AUC) metric. When analyzing the video recordings, you also discover that the model fails in highly congested traffic but
 works as expected when there is less traffic. What is the most likely reason for this result?
option_a: The model is overfitting in areas with less traffic and underfitting in areas with more traffic.
option_b: AUC is not the correct metric to evaluate this classification model.
option_c: Too much data representing congested areas was used for model training.
option_d: Gradients become small and vanish while backpropagating from the output to input nodes.
explanation: Performance that is good in light traffic but poor in congestion indicates that the model does not generalize to the congested slice, commonly because that condition is underrepresented or more complex. Option A is the closest answer, although calling the light-traffic behavior 'overfitting' is not proven without comparing training and validation performance.
exam_objectives: Monitoring, testing, and troubleshooting AI solutions
topics: Computer Vision; Evaluation Metrics; Classification; Clustering

question:
You are developing an ML model to predict house prices. While preparing the data, you discover that an important predictor variable, distance
 from the closest school, is often missing and does not have high variance. Every instance (row) in your data is important. How should you handle
 the missing data?
option_a: Delete the rows that have missing values.
option_b: Apply feature crossing with another column that does not have missing values.
option_c: Predict the missing values using linear regression.
option_d: Replace the missing values with zeros.
explanation: Rows cannot be discarded and zero is not a defensible value for distance. Predictive imputation using the other available features preserves every record and is appropriate for a continuous variable. The imputation model must be fit only on training data to avoid leakage.
exam_section: Collaborating within and across teams to manage data and models
exam_objectives: Exploring and preprocessing data for ML
topics: Feature Engineering; Regression; Data Preparation

question:
You are an ML engineer responsible for designing and implementing training pipelines for ML models. You need to create an end-to-end training
 pipeline for a TensorFlow model. The TensorFlow model will be trained on several terabytes of structured data. You need the pipeline to include
 data quality checks before training and model quality checks after training but prior to deployment. You want to minimize development time and
 the need for infrastructure maintenance. How should you build and orchestrate your training pipeline?
option_a:
Create the pipeline using Kubeflow Pipelines domain-specific language (DSL) and predefined Google Cloud components. Orchestrate the
 pipeline using Agent Platform Pipelines.
option_b: Create the pipeline using TensorFlow Extended (TFX) and standard TFX components. Orchestrate the pipeline using Agent Platform Pipelines.
option_c:
Create the pipeline using Kubeflow Pipelines domain-specific language (DSL) and predefined Google Cloud components. Orchestrate the
 pipeline using Kubeflow Pipelines deployed on Google Kubernetes Engine.
option_d:
Create the pipeline using TensorFlow Extended (TFX) and standard TFX components. Orchestrate the pipeline using Kubeflow Pipelines
 deployed on Google Kubernetes Engine.
explanation: TFX supplies standard components for schema and anomaly checks before training and model evaluation and validation before deployment. Agent Platform Pipelines runs the workflow as a managed service, minimizing infrastructure maintenance.
terminology_notes: Applied official direct product-name mappings only.

question:
You manage a team of data scientists who use a cloud-based backend system to submit training jobs. This system has become very difficult to
 administer, and you want to use a managed service instead. The data scientists you work with use many different frameworks, including Keras,
 PyTorch, theano, scikit-learn, and custom libraries. What should you do?
option_a: Use the Agent Platform Managed Training to submit training jobs using any framework.
option_b: Configure Kubeflow to run on Google Kubernetes Engine and submit training jobs through TFJob.
option_c: Create a library of VM images on Compute Engine, and publish these images on a centralized repository.
option_d: Set up Slurm workload manager to receive jobs that can be scheduled to run on your cloud infrastructure.
explanation: Agent Platform custom training accepts prebuilt or custom containers, allowing teams to submit jobs using different frameworks and private libraries without operating their own scheduler or Kubernetes cluster.

topics: Custom Training; Custom Containers; Agents; GKE

question:
You are training an object detection model using a Cloud TPU v2. Training time is taking longer than expected. Based on this simplified trace
 obtained with a Cloud TPU profile, what action should you take to decrease training time in a cost-efficient way?
option_a: Move from Cloud TPU v2 to Cloud TPU v3 and increase batch size.
option_b: Move from Cloud TPU v2 to 8 NVIDIA V100 GPUs and increase batch size.
option_c: Rewrite your input function to resize and reshape the input images.
option_d: Rewrite your input function using parallel reads, parallel processing, and prefetch.
explanation: A TPU trace showing idle compute time caused by input stalls should be addressed by optimizing the input pipeline. Parallel file reads, parallel map processing, and prefetch overlap preprocessing with accelerator execution and are more cost-efficient than switching hardware.
exam_objectives: Choosing appropriate hardware for training
topics: Training Hardware; Pipelines; Troubleshooting; Data Preparation

question:
While performing exploratory data analysis on a dataset, you find that an important categorical feature has 5% null values. You want to minimize
 the bias that could result from the missing values. How should you handle the missing values?
option_a: Remove the rows with missing values, and upsample your dataset by 5%.
option_b: Replace the missing values with the feature’s mean.
option_c: Replace the missing values with a placeholder category indicating a missing value.
option_d: Move the rows with missing values to your validation dataset.
explanation: For a categorical feature, a dedicated missing-value category preserves all rows and lets the model learn whether missingness itself carries information. A mean is undefined for categories, and moving missing rows into validation biases evaluation.
exam_section: Collaborating within and across teams to manage data and models
exam_objectives: Exploring and preprocessing data for ML
topics: Feature Engineering; Data Preparation; Responsible AI

question:
You are an ML engineer on an agricultural research team working on a crop disease detection tool to detect leaf rust spots in images of crops to
 determine the presence of a disease. These spots, which can vary in shape and size, are correlated to the severity of the disease. You want to
 develop a solution that predicts the presence and severity of the disease with high accuracy. What should you do?
option_a: Create an object detection model that can localize the rust spots.
option_b: Develop an image segmentation ML model to locate the boundaries of the rust spots.
option_c: Develop a template matching algorithm using traditional computer vision libraries.
option_d: Develop an image classification ML model to predict the presence of the disease.
explanation: Disease severity is correlated with the shape and area of rust spots. Image segmentation predicts pixel-level boundaries, enabling both presence detection and quantitative severity estimates. Object detection only provides bounding boxes.
exam_objectives: Building models given the task considering cost, complexity, latency, and scalability
topics: Clustering; Computer Vision; Evaluation Metrics; Classification

question:
You have been asked to productionize a proof-of-concept ML model built using Keras. The model was trained in a Jupyter notebook on a data
 scientist’s local machine. The notebook contains a cell that performs data validation and a cell that performs model analysis. You need to
 orchestrate the steps contained in the notebook and automate the execution of these steps for weekly retraining. You expect much more training
 data in the future. You want your solution to take advantage of managed services while minimizing cost. What should you do?
option_a:
Move the Jupyter notebook to a Notebooks instance on the largest N2 machine type, and schedule the execution of the steps in the
 Notebooks instance using Cloud Scheduler.
option_b:
Write the code as a TensorFlow Extended (TFX) pipeline orchestrated with Agent Platform Pipelines. Use standard TFX components for data
 validation and model analysis, and use Agent Platform Pipelines for model retraining.
option_c:
Rewrite the steps in the Jupyter notebook as an Apache Spark job, and schedule the execution of the job on ephemeral Dataproc clusters
 using Cloud Scheduler.
option_d:
Extract the steps contained in the Jupyter notebook as Python scripts, wrap each script in an Apache Airflow BashOperator, and run the
 resulting directed acyclic graph (DAG) in Cloud Composer.
explanation: TFX converts the notebook prototype into production components for data validation, training, and model analysis. Agent Platform Pipelines provides managed orchestration and ephemeral execution, scaling to larger future datasets without maintaining an always-on notebook or Airflow environment.
terminology_notes: Applied official direct product-name mappings only.
exam_objectives: Developing end-to-end ML pipelines; Exploring and preprocessing data for ML
topics: TFX; Pipelines; Agents; Dataproc

question:
You are working on a system log anomaly detection model for a cybersecurity organization. You have developed the model using TensorFlow, and
 you plan to use it for real-time prediction. You need to create a Dataflow pipeline to ingest data via Pub/Sub and write the results to BigQuery. You
 want to minimize the serving latency as much as possible. What should you do?
option_a: Load the model directly into the Dataflow job as a dependency, and use it for prediction.
option_b: Containerize the model prediction logic in Cloud Run, which is invoked by Dataflow.
option_c: Deploy the model to a Agent Platform endpoint, and invoke this endpoint in the Dataflow job.
option_d: Deploy the model in a TFServing container on Google Kubernetes Engine, and invoke it in the Dataflow job.
explanation: For minimum latency, load the TensorFlow model into the Dataflow workers and perform inference in-process, for example with Apache Beam RunInference. Calling Vertex AI, Cloud Run, or GKE introduces a network round trip for every inference request. The model must fit worker memory and be distributed efficiently.
terminology_notes: Generic or unrecognized Vertex AI reference requires contextual review.
exam_objectives: Serving models; Developing end-to-end ML pipelines
topics: Dataflow; Online Inference; Agents; AI Security

question:
You are an ML engineer at a mobile gaming company. A data scientist on your team recently trained a TensorFlow model, and you are responsible
 for deploying this model into a mobile application. You discover that the inference latency of the current model doesn’t meet production
 requirements. You need to reduce the inference time by 50%, and you are willing to accept a small decrease in model accuracy in order to reach
 the latency requirement. Without training a new model, which model optimization technique for reducing latency should you try first?
option_a: Weight pruning
option_b: Dynamic range quantization
option_c: Model distillation
option_d: Dimensionality reduction
explanation: Dynamic range quantization reduces model size and can improve CPU inference latency without retraining, usually with only a small accuracy impact. Pruning commonly requires retraining or fine-tuning, while distillation requires training a new student model.
exam_objectives: Serving models
topics: Model Optimization; Fine Tuning; Training Hardware; Custom Training

question:
You work on a data science team at a bank and are creating an ML model to predict loan default risk. You have collected and cleaned hundreds of
 millions of records worth of training data in a BigQuery table, and you now want to develop and compare multiple models on this data using
 TensorFlow and Vertex AI. You want to minimize any bottlenecks during the data ingestion state while considering scalability. What should you
 do?
option_a: Use the BigQuery client library to load data into a dataframe, and use tf.data.Dataset.from_tensor_slices() to read it.
option_b: Export data to CSV files in Cloud Storage, and use tf.data.TextLineDataset() to read them.
option_c: Convert the data into TFRecords, and use tf.data.TFRecordDataset() to read them.
option_d: Use TensorFlow I/O’s BigQuery Reader to directly read the data.
explanation: TensorFlow I/O's BigQuery connector can read BigQuery data directly into a tf.data pipeline and avoids materializing hundreds of millions of rows in a local dataframe or exporting intermediate CSV files. This is the most scalable direct-ingestion option listed.
terminology_notes: Generic or unrecognized Vertex AI reference requires contextual review.
exam_section: Collaborating within and across teams to manage data and models
exam_objectives: Exploring and preprocessing data for ML
topics: BigQuery; Custom Training; Pipelines; Cloud Storage

question:
You have recently created a proof-of-concept (POC) deep learning model. You are satisfied with the overall architecture, but you need to determine
 the value for a couple of hyperparameters. You want to perform hyperparameter tuning on Vertex AI to determine both the appropriate embedding
 dimension for a categorical feature used by your model and the optimal learning rate. You configure the following settings:
 • For the embedding dimension, you set the type to INTEGER with a minValue of 16 and maxValue of 64.
 • For the learning rate, you set the type to DOUBLE with a minValue of 10e-05 and maxValue of 10e-02.
 You are using the default Bayesian optimization tuning algorithm, and you want to maximize model accuracy. Training time is not a concern. How
 should you set the hyperparameter scaling for each hyperparameter and the maxParallelTrials?
option_a: Use UNIT_LINEAR_SCALE for the embedding dimension, UNIT_LOG_SCALE for the learning rate, and a large number of parallel trials.
option_b: Use UNIT_LINEAR_SCALE for the embedding dimension, UNIT_LOG_SCALE for the learning rate, and a small number of parallel trials.
option_c: Use UNIT_LOG_SCALE for the embedding dimension, UNIT_LINEAR_SCALE for the learning rate, and a large number of parallel trials.
option_d: Use UNIT_LOG_SCALE for the embedding dimension, UNIT_LINEAR_SCALE for the learning rate, and a small number of parallel trials.
explanation: Embedding dimension is a bounded integer over a relatively narrow range, so linear scaling is appropriate. Learning rates typically span orders of magnitude, so logarithmic scaling is appropriate. With Bayesian optimization and no urgency, fewer parallel trials preserve sequential learning between trials and generally improve search efficiency.
terminology_notes: Generic or unrecognized Vertex AI reference requires contextual review.
exam_objectives: Training models
topics: Hyperparameter Tuning; Embeddings; Evaluation Metrics; Model Optimization

question:
You are the Director of Data Science at a large company, and your Data Science team has recently begun using the Kubeflow Pipelines SDK to
 orchestrate their training pipelines. Your team is struggling to integrate their custom Python code into the Kubeflow Pipelines SDK. How should
 you instruct them to proceed in order to quickly integrate their code with the Kubeflow Pipelines SDK?
option_a: Use the func_to_container_op function to create custom components from the Python code.
option_b: Use the predefined components available in the Kubeflow Pipelines SDK to access Dataproc, and run the custom code there.
option_c:
Package the custom Python code into Docker containers, and use the load_component_from_file function to import the containers into the
 pipeline.
option_d: Deploy the custom Python code to Cloud Functions, and use Kubeflow Pipelines to trigger the Cloud Function.
explanation: For quick integration of existing Python functions, lightweight Python components convert a function into a containerized pipeline component with minimal boilerplate. In newer Kubeflow Pipelines versions, use the component decorator rather than the older func_to_container_op API.
exam_objectives: Developing end-to-end ML pipelines
topics: Kubeflow; Pipelines; Dataproc; Cloud Run

question:
You work for the AI team of an automobile company, and you are developing a visual defect detection model using TensorFlow and Keras. To
 improve your model performance, you want to incorporate some image augmentation functions such as translation, cropping, and contrast
 tweaking. You randomly apply these functions to each training batch. You want to optimize your data processing pipeline for run time and
 compute resources utilization. What should you do?
option_a: Embed the augmentation functions dynamically in the tf.Data pipeline.
option_b: Embed the augmentation functions dynamically as part of Keras generators.
option_c: Use Dataflow to create all possible augmentations, and store them as TFRecords.
option_d: Use Dataflow to create the augmentations dynamically per training run, and stage them as TFRecords.
explanation: Applying random augmentation in the tf.data input pipeline lets preprocessing run in parallel and be prefetched while producing new variants each epoch. Precomputing every augmentation greatly increases storage and loses the benefit of dynamic randomness.
exam_section: Collaborating within and across teams to manage data and models
exam_objectives: Exploring and preprocessing data for ML
topics: Data Preparation; Computer Vision; Dataflow; Pipelines

question:
You work for an online publisher that delivers news articles to over 50 million readers. You have built an AI model that recommends content for
 the company’s weekly newsletter. A recommendation is considered successful if the article is opened within two days of the newsletter’s
 published date and the user remains on the page for at least one minute.
 All the information needed to compute the success metric is available in BigQuery and is updated hourly. The model is trained on eight weeks of
 data, on average its performance degrades below the acceptable baseline after five weeks, and training time is 12 hours. You want to ensure that
 the model’s performance is above the acceptable baseline while minimizing cost. How should you monitor the model to determine when retraining
 is necessary?
option_a: Use Agent Platform Model Monitoring to detect skew of the input features with a sample rate of 100% and a monitoring frequency of two days.
option_b: Schedule a cron job in Cloud Tasks to retrain the model every week before the newsletter is created.
option_c: Schedule a weekly query in BigQuery to compute the success metric.
option_d: Schedule a daily Dataflow job in Cloud Composer to compute the success metric.
explanation: The business success metric is available in BigQuery and updates hourly. A scheduled weekly BigQuery query is sufficient to measure whether performance is approaching the five-week degradation point and is cheaper than daily Dataflow processing or retraining every week regardless of need.

question:
You deployed an ML model into production a year ago. Every month, you collect all raw requests that were sent to your model prediction service
 during the previous month. You send a subset of these requests to a human labeling service to evaluate your model’s performance. After a year,
 you notice that your model's performance sometimes degrades significantly after a month, while other times it takes several months to notice any
 decrease in performance. The labeling service is costly, but you also need to avoid large performance degradations. You want to determine how
 often you should retrain your model to maintain a high level of performance while minimizing cost. What should you do?
option_a:
Train an anomaly detection model on the training dataset, and run all incoming requests through this model. If an anomaly is detected,
 send the most recent serving data to the labeling service.
option_b:
Identify temporal patterns in your model’s performance over the previous year. Based on these patterns, create a schedule for sending
 serving data to the labeling service for the next year.
option_c:
Compare the cost of the labeling service with the lost revenue due to model performance degradation over the past year. If the lost revenue
 is greater than the cost of the labeling service, increase the frequency of model retraining; otherwise, decrease the model retraining frequency.
option_d:
Run training-serving skew detection batch jobs every few days to compare the aggregate statistics of the features in the training dataset
 with recent serving data. If skew is detected, send the most recent serving data to the labeling service.
explanation: Frequent training-serving skew checks are relatively inexpensive and can trigger costly human labeling only when the serving distribution changes. Human labels are still needed to confirm actual performance degradation before retraining. Skew is only a proxy, so this design should also retain periodic quality checks.
exam_objectives: Monitoring, testing, and troubleshooting AI solutions; Automating model retraining
topics: Model Monitoring; Pipelines; Time Series

question:
You work for a company that manages a ticketing platform for a large chain of cinemas. Customers use a mobile app to search for movies they’re
 interested in and purchase tickets in the app. Ticket purchase requests are sent to Pub/Sub and are processed with a Dataflow streaming pipeline
 configured to conduct the following steps:
 1. Check for availability of the movie tickets at the selected cinema.
 2. Assign the ticket price and accept payment.
 3. Reserve the tickets at the selected cinema.
 4. Send successful purchases to your database.
 Each step in this process has low latency requirements (less than 50 milliseconds). You have developed a logistic regression model with BigQuery
 ML that predicts whether offering a promo code for free popcorn increases the chance of a ticket purchase, and this prediction should be added
 to the ticket purchase process. You want to identify the simplest way to deploy this model to production while adding minimal latency. What
 should you do?
option_a: Run batch inference with BigQuery ML every five minutes on each new set of tickets issued.
option_b: Export your model in TensorFlow format, and add a tfx_bsl.public.beam.RunInference step to the Dataflow pipeline.
option_c: Export your model in TensorFlow format, deploy it on Vertex AI, and query the prediction endpoint from your streaming pipeline.
option_d:
Convert your model with TensorFlow Lite (TFLite), and add it to the mobile app so that the promo code and the incoming request arrive
 together in Pub/Sub.
explanation: The prediction must be added to an existing low-latency Dataflow stream. Exporting the BigQuery ML logistic-regression model and running inference inside the Beam workers avoids a network call for each event and is simpler and lower-latency than a remote endpoint. The modern Beam API is RunInference.
terminology_notes: Generic or unrecognized Vertex AI reference requires contextual review.
exam_objectives: Serving models; Developing end-to-end ML pipelines
topics: Dataflow; BigQuery ML; Online Inference; BigQuery

question:
You work on a team in a data center that is responsible for server maintenance. Your management team wants you to build a predictive
 maintenance solution that uses monitoring data to detect potential server failures. Incident data has not been labeled yet. What should you do
 first?
option_a:
Train a time-series model to predict the machines’ performance values. Configure an alert if a machine’s actual performance values
 significantly differ from the predicted performance values.
option_b:
Develop a simple heuristic (e.g., based on z-score) to label the machines’ historical performance data. Use this heuristic to monitor server
 performance in real time.
option_c:
Develop a simple heuristic (e.g., based on z-score) to label the machines’ historical performance data. Train a model to predict anomalies
 based on this labeled dataset.
option_d:
Hire a team of qualified analysts to review and label the machines’ historical performance data. Train a model based on this manually
 labeled dataset.
explanation: Because incidents are unlabeled, begin with a simple interpretable anomaly heuristic to establish provisional labels and operational baselines. This is faster and cheaper than immediately commissioning a large labeling effort or training a supervised model from unvalidated pseudo-labels.
exam_objectives: Building models given the task considering cost, complexity, latency, and scalability
topics: Classification; Model Optimization

question:
You work for a retailer that sells clothes to customers around the world. You have been tasked with ensuring that ML models are built in a secure
 manner. Specifically, you need to protect sensitive customer data that might be used in the models. You have identified four fields containing
 sensitive data that are being used by your data science team: AGE, IS_EXISTING_CUSTOMER, LATITUDE_LONGITUDE, and SHIRT_SIZE. What
 should you do with the data before it is made available to the data science team for training purposes?
option_a: Tokenize all of the fields using hashed dummy values to replace the real values.
option_b: Use principal component analysis (PCA) to reduce the four sensitive fields to one PCA vector.
option_c:
Coarsen the data by putting AGE into quantiles and rounding LATITUDE_LONGTTUDE into single precision. The other two fields are already
 as coarse as possible.
option_d: Remove all sensitive data fields, and ask the data science team to build their models using non-sensitive data.
explanation: Coarsening age and geolocation reduces re-identification risk while preserving useful predictive signal. Tokenizing numeric and ordinal fields would destroy important relationships, PCA is not a privacy control, and removing every field may unnecessarily reduce model utility. A formal privacy review and tools such as Sensitive Data Protection are still required.
exam_objectives: Identifying risks to AI solutions
topics: Data Privacy; Feature Engineering; Vector Search; Evaluation Metrics

question:
You work for a magazine publisher and have been tasked with predicting whether customers will cancel their annual subscription. In your
 exploratory data analysis, you find that 90% of individuals renew their subscription every year, and only 10% of individuals cancel their
 subscription. After training a NN Classifier, your model predicts those who cancel their subscription with 99% accuracy and predicts those who
 renew their subscription with 82% accuracy. How should you interpret these results?
option_a:
This is not a good result because the model should have a higher accuracy for those who renew their subscription than for those who
 cancel their subscription.
option_b: This is not a good result because the model is performing worse than predicting that people will always renew their subscription.
option_c: This is a good result because predicting those who cancel their subscription is more difficult, since there is less data for this group.
option_d: This is a good result because the accuracy across both groups is greater than 80%.
explanation: Using the stated per-class accuracies, overall accuracy is about 83.7%: 0.9×0.82 + 0.1×0.99. A trivial classifier that always predicts renewal would achieve 90% overall accuracy, so the model is worse on aggregate despite strong performance on the minority class. Class-specific recall, precision, and business costs should also be examined.
exam_objectives: Monitoring, testing, and troubleshooting AI solutions
topics: Data Preparation; Evaluation Metrics; Classification; Model Monitoring

question:
You have built a model that is trained on data stored in Parquet files. You access the data through a Hive table hosted on Google Cloud. You
 preprocessed these data with PySpark and exported it as a CSV file into Cloud Storage. After preprocessing, you execute additional steps to train
 and evaluate your model. You want to parametrize this model training in Kubeflow Pipelines. What should you do?
option_a: Remove the data transformation step from your pipeline.
option_b: Containerize the PySpark transformation step, and add it to your pipeline.
option_c:
Add a ContainerOp to your pipeline that spins a Dataproc cluster, runs a transformation, and then saves the transformed data in Cloud
 Storage.
option_d:
Deploy Apache Spark at a separate node pool in a Google Kubernetes Engine cluster. Add a ContainerOp to your pipeline that invokes a
 corresponding transformation job for this Spark instance.
explanation: The PySpark transformation should remain a reproducible pipeline step. A pipeline component can create an ephemeral Dataproc cluster, run the Spark transformation, write the result to Cloud Storage, and then tear the cluster down. This avoids maintaining a permanent Spark node pool.

question:
You have developed an ML model to detect the sentiment of users’ posts on your company's social media page to identify outages or bugs. You
 are using Dataflow to provide real-time predictions on data ingested from Pub/Sub. You plan to have multiple training iterations for your model
 and keep the latest two versions live after every run. You want to split the traffic between the versions in an 80:20 ratio, with the newest model
 getting the majority of the traffic. You want to keep the pipeline as simple as possible, with minimal management required. What should you do?
option_a: Deploy the models to a Agent Platform endpoint using the traffic-split=0=80, PREVIOUS_MODEL_ID=20 configuration.
option_b: Wrap the models inside an App Engine application using the --splits PREVIOUS_VERSION=0.2, NEW_VERSION=0.8 configuration
option_c: Wrap the models inside a Cloud Run container using the REVISION1=20, REVISION2=80 revision configuration.
option_d: Implement random splitting in Dataflow using beam.Partition() with a partition function calling a Agent Platform endpoint.
explanation: A Agent Platform endpoint supports weighted traffic splitting across deployed models, so the latest and previous versions can receive 80% and 20% of traffic without adding custom routing logic to Dataflow or operating App Engine or Cloud Run wrappers.

question:
You are developing an image recognition model using PyTorch based on ResNet50 architecture. Your code is working fine on your local laptop on
 a small subsample. Your full dataset has 200k labeled images. You want to quickly scale your training workload while minimizing cost. You plan
 to use 4 V100 GPUs. What should you do?
option_a: Create a Google Kubernetes Engine cluster with a node pool that has 4 V100 GPUs. Prepare and submit a TFJob operator to this node pool.
option_b: Create a Agent Platform Workbench user-managed notebooks instance with 4 V100 GPUs, and use it to train your model.
option_c:
Package your code with Setuptools, and use a pre-built container. Train your model with Vertex AI using a custom tier that contains the
 required GPUs.
option_d:
Configure a Compute Engine VM with all the dependencies that launches the training. Train your model with Vertex AI using a custom tier
 that contains the required GPUs.
explanation: Agent Platform custom training with a prebuilt PyTorch container and a custom machine specification provisions the four GPUs only for the job and avoids managing a GKE cluster or a persistent notebook VM. Packaging the training application is the standard managed approach.

question:
You have trained a DNN regressor with TensorFlow to predict housing prices using a set of predictive features. Your default precision is tf.float64,
 and you use a standard TensorFlow estimator:
 Your model performs well, but just before deploying it to production, you discover that your current serving latency is 10ms @ 90 percentile and
 you currently serve on CPUs. Your production requirements expect a model latency of 8ms @ 90 percentile. You're willing to accept a small
 decrease in performance in order to reach the latency requirement.
 Therefore your plan is to improve latency while evaluating how much the model's prediction decreases. What should you first try to quickly lower
 the serving latency?
option_a: Switch from CPU to GPU serving.
option_b: Apply quantization to your SavedModel by reducing the floating point precision to tf.float16.
option_c: Increase the dropout rate to 0.8 and retrain your model.
option_d: Increase the dropout rate to 0.8 in _PREDICT mode by adjusting the TensorFlow Serving parameters.
explanation: Reducing numerical precision can lower model size and improve inference latency while usually causing only a small accuracy change. GPU serving often adds overhead for small low-latency models, and dropout is disabled during inference and therefore does not provide the proposed latency improvement. Validate that the target serving hardware benefits from float16.
exam_objectives: Scaling online model serving

question:
You work on the data science team at a manufacturing company. You are reviewing the company’s historical sales data, which has hundreds of
 millions of records. For your exploratory data analysis, you need to calculate descriptive statistics such as mean, median, and mode; conduct
 complex statistical tests for hypothesis testing; and plot variations of the features over time. You want to use as much of the sales data as
 possible in your analyses while minimizing computational resources. What should you do?
option_a:
Visualize the time plots in Google Data Studio. Import the dataset into Vertex Al Workbench user-managed notebooks. Use this data to
 calculate the descriptive statistics and run the statistical analyses.
option_b:
Spin up a Vertex Al Workbench user-managed notebooks instance and import the dataset. Use this data to create statistical and visual
 analyses.
option_c:
Use BigQuery to calculate the descriptive statistics. Use Vertex Al Workbench user-managed notebooks to visualize the time plots and run
 the statistical analyses.
option_d:
Use BigQuery to calculate the descriptive statistics, and use Google Data Studio to visualize the time plots. Use Vertex Al Workbench user-
 managed notebooks to run the statistical analyses.
explanation: BigQuery should perform scalable descriptive aggregations over hundreds of millions of rows. A managed notebook can query BigQuery for samples or aggregate results, run specialized statistical tests, and create custom plots without importing the full raw dataset into notebook memory.

question:

 accuracy metrics for various experiments and use an API to query the metrics over time. What should they use to track and report their
 experiments while minimizing manual effort?
option_a: Use Vertex Al Pipelines to execute the experiments. Query the results stored in MetadataStore using the Vertex Al API.
option_b: Use Vertex Al Training to execute the experiments. Write the accuracy metrics to BigQuery, and query the results using the BigQuery API.

Use Vertex Al Training to execute the experiments. Write the accuracy metrics to Cloud Monitoring, and query the results using the
 Monitoring API.
option_d:
Use Vertex Al Workbench user-managed notebooks to execute the experiments. Collect the results in a shared Google Sheets file, and query
 the results using the Google Sheets API.
explanation: Agent Platform Pipelines records pipeline executions, parameters, artifacts, and metrics in Agent Platform ML Metadata, which can be queried through Vertex AI APIs. This minimizes custom experiment-tracking code. Experiments on Agent Platform is the newer dedicated interface for comparing runs.

question:
You are training an ML model using data stored in BigQuery that contains several values that are considered Personally Identifiable Information
 (PII). You need to reduce the sensitivity of the dataset before training your model. Every column is critical to your model. How should you
 proceed?
option_a: Using Dataflow, ingest the columns with sensitive data from BigQuery, and then randomize the values in each sensitive column.
option_b:
Use the Cloud Data Loss Prevention (DLP) API to scan for sensitive data, and use Dataflow with the DLP API to encrypt sensitive values
 with Format Preserving Encryption.
option_c:
Use the Cloud Data Loss Prevention (DLP) API to scan for sensitive data, and use Dataflow to replace all sensitive data by using the
 encryption algorithm AES-256 with a salt.
option_d:
Before training, use BigQuery to select only the columns that do not contain sensitive data. Create an authorized view of the data so that
 sensitive values cannot be accessed by unauthorized individuals.
explanation: Format-preserving or deterministic encryption can de-identify sensitive values while preserving column shape and joinability when configured correctly. Randomizing values destroys relationships, and removing critical columns violates the stated requirement. Key management and re-identification risk must be reviewed carefully.

question:
You recently deployed an ML model. Three months after deployment, you notice that your model is underperforming on certain subgroups, thus
 potentially leading to biased results. You suspect that the inequitable performance is due to class imbalances in the training data, but you cannot
 collect more data. What should you do? (Choose two.)
option_a: Remove training examples of high-performing subgroups, and retrain the model.
option_b: Add an additional objective to penalize the model more for errors made on the minority class, and retrain the model
option_c: Remove the features that have the highest correlations with the majority class.
option_d: Upsample or reweight your existing training data, and retrain the model
option_e: Redeploy the model, and provide a label explaining the model's behavior to users.
explanation: Cost-sensitive learning can penalize errors on the minority group more heavily, and reweighting or upsampling can correct representation imbalance without collecting new examples. Removing majority examples may discard useful data, while removing correlated features does not directly solve unequal error rates.
exam_objectives: Identifying risks to AI solutions
topics: Responsible AI; Data Preparation

question:
You are working on a binary classification ML algorithm that detects whether an image of a classified scanned document contains a company’s
 logo. In the dataset, 96% of examples don’t have the logo, so the dataset is very skewed. Which metric would give you the most confidence in your
 model?
option_a: Precision
option_b: Recall
option_c: RMSE
option_d: F1 score
explanation: With only 4% positive examples, accuracy is misleading. F1 combines precision and recall and is appropriate when both false positives and false negatives matter. If one error type is substantially more costly, a threshold-specific precision, recall, or F-beta metric would be better.
exam_objectives: Monitoring, testing, and troubleshooting AI solutions
topics: Evaluation Metrics; Data Preparation; Computer Vision; Classification

question:
While running a model training pipeline on Vertex Al, you discover that the evaluation step is failing because of an out-of-memory error. You are
 currently using TensorFlow Model Analysis (TFMA) with a standard Evaluator TensorFlow Extended (TFX) pipeline component for the evaluation
 step. You want to stabilize the pipeline without downgrading the evaluation quality while minimizing infrastructure overhead. What should you do?
option_a: Include the flag -runner=DataflowRunner in beam_pipeline_args to run the evaluation step on Dataflow.
option_b: Move the evaluation step out of your pipeline and run it on custom Compute Engine VMs with sufficient memory.
option_c:
Migrate your pipeline to Kubeflow hosted on Google Kubernetes Engine, and specify the appropriate node parameters for the evaluation
 step.
option_d: Add tfma.MetricsSpec () to limit the number of metrics in the evaluation step.
explanation: Running the TFMA evaluation on Dataflow distributes Beam processing and provides scalable memory and compute without requiring the team to operate custom VMs or a GKE cluster. Reducing metrics would lower evaluation coverage, contrary to the requirement.
